variantrule.name: Ability Check
entries: An {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} tests a character's or monster's innate talent and training in an effort to overcome a challenge. The GM calls for an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} when a character or monster attempts an action (other than an attack) that has a chance of failure. When the outcome is uncertain, the dice determine the results.

For every {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, the GM decides which of the six abilities is relevant to the task at hand and the difficulty of the task, represented by Difficulty Class (DC). The more difficult a task, the higher its DC. The Ability Check DCs table shows common DCs.

To make an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, roll a {@dice d20} and add the relevant ability modifier. As with other {@dice d20} rolls, apply bonuses and penalties, and compare the total to the DC. If the total equals or exceeds the DC, the {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} is a success—the creature overcomes the challenge at hand. Otherwise, it's a failure, which means the character or monster makes no progress toward the objective or makes progress combined with a setback determined by the GM.

variantrule.name: Saving Throw
entries: A {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}-also called a save-represents an attempt to resist a power, a trap, a poison, a disease, or a similar threat. You don't normally decide to make a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}; you are forced to make one because your character or monster is at risk of harm.

To make a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, roll a {@dice d20} and add the appropriate ability modifier. For example, you use your Dexterity modifier for a Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}.

A {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} can be modified by a situational bonus or penalty and can be affected by {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}, as determined by the GM.

Each class gives proficiency in at least two {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}. The operative, for example, is proficient in Intelligence saves. As with skill proficiencies, proficiency in a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} lets a character add his or her {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} made using a particular ability score. Some monsters have {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} proficiencies as well.

The Difficulty Class for a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} is determined by the effect that causes it. For example, the DC for a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} allowed by a power is determined by the caster's force- or tech-casting ability and {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}.

The result of a successful or failed {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} is also detailed in the effect that allows the save. Usually, a successful save means that a creature suffers no harm, or reduced harm, from an effect.

variantrule.name: Advantage
entries: Sometimes a special ability or power tells you that you have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, or an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}. When that happens, you roll a second {@dice d20} when you make the roll. Use the higher of the two rolls if you have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}.

If multiple situations affect a roll and each one grants {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} or imposes {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on it, you don't roll more than one additional {@dice d20}. If two favorable situations grant {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, for example, you still roll only one additional {@dice d20}.

If circumstances cause a roll to have both {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}, you are considered to have neither of them, and you roll one {@dice d20}.

variantrule.name: Disadvantage
entries: Sometimes a special ability or power tells you that you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, or an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}. When that happens, you roll a second {@dice d20} when you make the roll. Use the lower of the two rolls if you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}.

If multiple situations affect a roll and each one grants {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} or imposes {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on it, you don't roll more than one additional {@dice d20}.

If circumstances cause a roll to have both {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}, you are considered to have neither of them, and you roll one {@dice d20}.

variantrule.name: Attack Roll
entries: When you make an attack, your {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} determines whether the attack hits or misses. To make an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, roll a {@dice d20} and add the appropriate modifiers. If the total of the roll plus modifiers equals or exceeds the target's {@variantrule Armor Class|sw5e-phb} (AC), the attack hits. The AC of a character is determined at character creation, whereas the AC of a creature is in its stat block.

entries.name: Modifiers to the Roll
entries: When a character makes an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, the two most common modifiers to the roll are an ability modifier and the character's {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}. When a creature makes an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, it uses whatever modifier is provided in its stat block.

{@b {@i Ability Modifier.}} The ability modifier used for a {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack} is Strength, and the ability modifier used for a ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack} is Dexterity. Weapons that have the finesse or thrown property break this rule.

Some powers also require an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}. The ability modifier used for a power attack depends on the force- or tech-casting ability of the force- or tech-caster, as explained in {@book chapter 10|sw5e-phb|10}.

{@b {@i Proficiency Bonus.}} You add your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to your {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} when you attack using a weapon with which you have proficiency, as well as when you attack with a power.

entries.name: Rolling 1 or 20
entries: Sometimes fate blesses or curses a combatant, causing the novice to hit and the veteran to miss.

If the {@dice d20} roll for an attack is a 20, the attack hits regardless of any modifiers or the target's AC. In addition, the attack is a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit}, as explained later in this chapter.
If the {@dice d20} roll for an attack is a 1, the attack misses regardless of any modifiers or the target's AC.

entries.name: Choosing to be Hit
entries: Sometimes, an attack might miss you when you wanted it to hit. You can choose to allow a miss to hit you (no action required). If you do so, the attacker chooses the maximum amount of damage instead of rolling.

variantrule.name: Armor Class
entries: Your {@b Armor Class} (AC) represents how well your character avoids being wounded in battle. Things that contribute to your AC include the armor you wear, the {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shield} you carry, and your Dexterity modifier. Not all characters wear armor or carry {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shields}, however.

Without armor or a {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shield}, your character's AC equals 10 + his or her Dexterity modifier. If your character wears armor, carries a {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shield}, or both, calculate your AC using the rules in {@book Equipment|sw5e-phb|5}. Record your AC on your character sheet.

Your character needs to be proficient with armor and shields to wear and use them effectively, and your armor and {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shield} proficiencies are determined by your class. There are drawbacks to wearing armor or carrying a {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shield} if you lack the required proficiency, as explained in {@book Equipment|sw5e-phb|5}.
Some powers and class features give you a different way to calculate your AC. If you have multiple features that give you different ways to calculate your AC, you choose which one to use.

variantrule.name: Bonus Action
entries: Various class features, powers, and other abilities let you take an additional action on your turn called a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}. The Cunning Action feature, for example, allows an operative to take a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}. You can take a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} only when a special ability, power, or other feature of the game states that you can do something as a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}. You otherwise don't have a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to take.
You can take only one {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} on your turn, so you must choose which {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to use when you have more than one available.

You choose when to take a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} during your turn, unless the {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}'s timing is specified, and anything that deprives you of your ability to take actions also prevents you from taking a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}.

variantrule.name: Reaction
entries: Certain special abilities, powers, and situations allow you to take a special action called a {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}. A {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}, typically an instant response to a trigger of some kind, can occur on your turn or on someone else's. The {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack}, described later in this chapter, is the most common type of {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}.

When you take a {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}, you can't take another one until the start of your next turn. If the {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} interrupts another creature's turn, that creature can continue its turn right after the {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}.
Certain features, such as the scholar's Multitasker, might grant you an additional {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}. If you have two or more reactions, you can only take one per turn.

variantrule.name: Critical Hit
entries: When you score a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit}, you get to roll all of the attack's damage dice twice, including any additional damage dice, and add them together. Then add any relevant modifiers as normal. To {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} up play, you can roll all the damage dice at once.

{@b {@i Critical Hit Range.}} The {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} range of an effect determines on what {@dice d20} results that effect scores a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit}. Typically, an effect has a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} range of 1, meaning it only scores a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} on a 20. A {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} range of 2, however, would mean the effect scores a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} on a roll of 19 or 20. A {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} range cannot exceed 5, scoring a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} on 16-20.

variantrule.name: Hit Points
entries: Your Constitution modifier contributes to your {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. Typically, you add your Constitution modifier to each Hit Die you roll for your {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}.

If your Constitution modifier changes, your hit point maximum changes as well, as though you had the new modifier from 1st level. For example, if you raise your Constitution score when you reach 4th level and your Constitution modifier increases from +1 to +2, you adjust your hit point maximum as though the modifier had always been +2. So you add 3 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} for your first three levels, and then roll your {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} for 4th level using your new modifier. Or if you're 7th level and some effect lowers your Constitution score so as to reduce your Constitution modifier by 1, your hit point maximum is reduced by 7.

variantrule.name: Short Rest
entries: A {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest} is a period of downtime, at least 1 hour long, during which a character does nothing more strenuous than eating, drinking, reading, and tending to wounds.

A character can spend one or more Hit Dice at the end of a {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest}, up to the character's maximum number of Hit Dice, which is equal to the character's level. Whenever a character spends a Hit Die to regain {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, the player rolls the die and adds the character's Constitution modifier to it. The character regains {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} equal to the total. The player can decide to spend an additional Hit Die after each roll.

variantrule.name: Long Rest
entries: A {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest} is a period of extended downtime, at least 8 hours long, during which a character sleeps for at least 6 hours and performs light activity, such as reading, talking, eating, or standing watch, for no more than 2 hours. If the rest is interrupted by a period of strenuous activity—fighting, casting powers, at least 1 hour of walking, or similar adventuring activity—the characters must restart the rest to benefit from it.

At the end of a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}, a character regains all lost {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. The character also regains spent Hit Dice, up to a number of dice equal to half of the character's total number of them (minimum of one).

A character can't benefit from more than one {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest} in a 24-hour period, and a character must have at least 1 hit point at the start of the rest to gain its benefits.

entries.name: Variant: Resting in Armor
entries: Resting in armor makes it difficult to recover fully. At the end of a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}, if you wore your armor, you only recover one-quarter your spent Hit Dice (minimum of one), instead of half.

variantrule.name: Proficiency
entries: Characters have a {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} determined by level, as detailed in {@book chapter 1|sw5e-phb|1}. Monsters also have this bonus, which is incorporated in their stat blocks. The bonus is used in the rules on {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability checks}, {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}, and {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls}.

Your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} can't be added to a single die roll or other number more than once. For example, if two different rules say you can add your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to a Wisdom {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, you nevertheless add the bonus only once when you make the save.

Occasionally, your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} might be multiplied or divided (doubled or halved. for example) before you apply it. If a circumstance suggests that your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} applies more than once to the same roll, you still add it only once and multiply or divide it only once.

By the same token, if a feature or effect allows you to multiply your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} when making an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} that wouldn't normally benefit from your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}, you still don't add the bonus to the check. For that check your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} is 0, given the fact that multiplying 0 by any number is still 0. For instance, if you lack proficiency in the {@skill Lore|sw5e-phb} skill, you gain no benefit from a feature that lets you double your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} when you make Intelligence ({@skill Lore|sw5e-phb}) checks.

In general, you don't multiply your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} for {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} or {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}. If a feature or effect allows you to do so, these same rules apply.

entries.name: Expertise
entries: Certain features, such as the {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb} class feature or {@feat Ace Pilot|sw5e-phb} feat, grant {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in a skill or tool, letting you double your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} with that skill or tool. As usual, you can only gain {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in a skill or tool once.

Far less common, though still possible, a creature can gain {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}. Creatures cannot gain {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in weapons, however.

variantrule.name: Speed
entries: Your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} determines how far you can move when traveling ({@book chapter 8|sw5e-phb|8}) and fighting ({@book chapter 9|sw5e-phb|9}).

variantrule.name: Initiative
entries: At the beginning of every combat, you roll {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} by making a Dexterity check. {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb} determines the order of creatures' turns in combat, as described in {@book chapter 9|sw5e-phb|9}.

entries.name: Hiding
entries: hen you try to hide, make a Dexterity ({@skill Stealth|sw5e-phb}) check. Until you are discovered or you stop hiding, that checks total is contested by the Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) check of any creature that actively searches for signs of your presence. You can't hide from a creature that can see you, and if you make noise (such as shouting a warning or knocking over a vase), you give away your position. An {@condition Invisible|sw5e-phb|invisible} creature can't be seen, so it can always try to hide. Signs of its passage might still be noticed, however, and it still has to stay quiet. In combat, most creatures stay alert for signs of danger all around, so if you come out of hiding and approach a creature, it usually sees you. However, under certain circumstances, the Dungeon Master might allow you to stay hidden as you approach a creature that is distracted, allowing you to gain {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on an attack before you are seen. {@b {@i Passive Perception.}} When you hide, there's a chance someone will notice you even if they aren't searching. To determine whether such a creature notices you, the GM compares your Dexterity ({@skill Stealth|sw5e-phb}) check with that creature's passive Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) score, which equals 10 + the creature's Wisdom modifier, as well as any other bonuses or penalties. If the creature has {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, add 5. For {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}, subtract 5. For example, if a lst-level character (with a {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} of +2) has a Wisdom of 15 (a +2 modifier) and proficiency in {@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}, he or she has a passive Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) of 14. {@b {@i What Can You See?}} One of the main factors in determining whether you can find a hidden creature or object is how well you can see in an area, which might be {@b lightly} or {@b heavily} obscured, as explained in {@book chapter 8|sw5e-phb|8}.

variantrule.name: Death Saving Throw
entries: Whenever you start your turn with 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, you must make a special {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, called a {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throw}, to determine whether you creep closer to death or hang onto life. Unlike other {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}, this one isn't tied to any ability score. You are in the hands of fate now, aided only by powers and features that improve your chances of succeeding on a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}. Roll a {@dice d20}. If the roll is 10 or higher, you succeed. Otherwise, you fail. A success or failure has no effect by itself. On your third success, you become stable (see below). On your third failure, you die. The successes and failures don't need to be consecutive; keep track of both until you collect three of a kind. The number of both is reset to zero when you regain any {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} or become stable.

{@b {@i Rolling 1 or 20.}} When you make a {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throw} and roll a 1 on the {@dice d20}, it counts as two failures. If you roll a 20 on the {@dice d20}, you regain 1 hit point.

{@b {@i Damage at 0 Hit Points.}} If you take any damage while you have 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} (for example, by catching fire because your limbs were all chopped off next to a pit of lava), you suffer a {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throw} failure. If the damage is from a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit}, you suffer two failures instead. If the damage equals or exceeds your hit point maximum, you suffer instant death.

variantrule.name: Unarmed Strike
entries: Regardless of whether or not you are armed, you can fight in melee by making an unarmed strike. Your {@variantrule Unarmed Strike|sw5e-phb|unarmed strikes} are a weapon with which you are proficient and, unless otherwise indicated, they do 1 + your Strength modifier kinetic damage.

variantrule.name: Cover
entries: Walls, trees, creatures, and other obstacles can {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|provide cover} during combat, making a target more difficult to harm. A target can benefit from {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} only when an attack or other effect originates on the opposite side of the {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover}.

There are four degrees of {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover}. If a target is behind multiple sources of {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover}, only the most protective degree of {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} applies, not added together.

A target with {@b one-quarter cover} has a +2 bonus to AC and Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}. A target has one-quarter {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} if an obstacle blocks at least one-fourth of its body, such as a thin pillar or a creature of one size category smaller.

A target with {@b half cover} has a +3 bonus to AC and Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}. A target has {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|half cover} if an obstacle blocks at least half of its body, such as a low wall or a creature of the same size category.

A target with {@b three-quarters cover} has a +5 bonus to AC and Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}. A target has three-quarter {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} if about three-quarters of it is obstructed, whether by an obstacle or a creature of one size category larger.

A target with {@b total cover} can't be targeted directly by an attack or a power, although some powers can reach such a target by including it in an area of effect. A target has {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|total cover} if it is completely concealed by an obstacle.

entries.name: Variant: Creatures Providing Cover
entries: Sometimes, creatures in close proximity create a veritable mess of bodies, potentially causing attacks targeting one to hit another. Using this variant, if an attack would miss a creature by an amount less than or equal to the bonus to AC granted by the {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} of another creature, and the attack would hit that other creature, the GM might consider having that other creature take the attack's damage.

variantrule.name: Difficult Terrain
entries: Combat rarely takes place in bare rooms or on featureless plains. Boulder-strewn caverns, briar-choked forests, treacherous staircases—the setting of a typical fight contains {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain}.

Every foot of movement in {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain} costs 1 extra foot. This rule is true even if multiple things in a space count as {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain}.

Low furniture, rubble, undergrowth, steep stairs, snow, and shallow bogs are examples of {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain}. The space of another creature, whether hostile or not, also counts as {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain}.

variantrule.name: Expertise
entries: Certain features, such as the {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb} class feature or {@feat Ace Pilot|sw5e-phb} feat, grant {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in a skill or tool, letting you double your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} with that skill or tool. As usual, you can only gain {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in a skill or tool once.

Far less common, though still possible, a creature can gain {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}. Creatures cannot gain {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in weapons, however.

variantrule.name: Concentration
entries: Some powers require you to maintain {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration} in order to keep their effect active. If you lose {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration}, such a power ends.

If a power must be maintained with {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration}, that fact appears in its Duration entry, and the power specifies how long you can concentrate on it. You can end {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration} at any time (no action required).

Normal activity, such as moving and attacking, doesn't interfere with {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration}. The following factors can break {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration}:

The GM might also decide that certain environmental phenomena, such as {@spell Turbulence|sw5e-phb|turbulence} on a ship or rocky terrain on a speeder, require you to succeed on a DC 10 Constitution {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} to maintain {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration} on a power.

variantrule.name: Acid
entries: Vials of corrosive liquid or the {@i acid splash} {@book tech power|sw5e-phb|12|Tech Powers} deal acid damage.

variantrule.name: Cold
entries: The chill energy of carbonite and cryogenesis deal cold damage.

variantrule.name: Energy
entries: Energy damage is the damage dealt by {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons, {@filter lightweapons|items|type=martial weapon|category=lightweapon}, and other powers or abilities.

variantrule.name: Fire
entries: The concussive damage of an explosion or an open flame deal fire damage.

variantrule.name: Force
entries: Certain {@book force powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} that channel the pure energy of the Force deal force damage.

variantrule.name: Ion
entries: Ion damage is a special damage type that is most effective against droids and constructs. Simple electronics dealt ion damage are disabled until rebooted, unless that damage would destroy them outright.

variantrule.name: Kinetic
entries: Kinetic damage encompasses all physical damage commonly dealt by {@filter vibroweapons|items|type=martial weapon}.

variantrule.name: Lightning
entries: The electrifying energy of the {@i force lightning} power deals lightning damage.

variantrule.name: Necrotic
entries: Necrotic damage, dealt by powers like {@i death field}, withers matter and even the soul.

variantrule.name: Poison
entries: Venomous stings and the toxic {@i poison spray} power deal poison damage.

variantrule.name: Psychic
entries: The crippling agony caused by powers like {@i feedback} deal psychic damage.

variantrule.name: Sonic
entries: Debilitating noises cause sonic damage.

variantrule.name: True
entries: True damage is not dealt by any specific source. Instead, effects that prevent or redirect damage cannot be used to counter the loss of life caused by true damage.
